list.listitem: Patients with a parapneumonic effusion greater than 1 cm on lateral decubitus chest x-ray should have a thoracentesis performed for diagnostic (and therapeutic) purposes. C
Patients with unilateral pleural effusion should have CT to evaluate for malignancy and imaging guided thoracentesis for culture, cytology, and biomarkers. C

Customarily, an effusion is exudative if: (1) the ratio of protein in the pleural fluid to serum protein is greater than 0.5; (2) the ratio of the level of lactated dehydrogenase (LDH) in the pleural fluid to serum LDH is greater than 0.6; or (3) the absolute level of LDH in the pleural fluid is greater than two-thirds of the upper limit of local laboratory normal value. C
Pleural cholesterol >55 mg/dl, pleural LDL >200 U/L, and ratio of pleural cholesterol to serum cholesterol >0.3 were the most accurate predictors of exudative effusion in a systematic review.
The routine use of fibrinolytics to drain parapneumonic effusions is not recommended. B
Rapid drainage of complicated parapneumonic effusions prevents undue morbidity and mortality. B

For malignant pleural effusion, in patients with expandable lungs either USN guided large volume thoracentesis using an indwelling cathter or talc pleurodesis are options; if unexpandable, indwelling catheter is preferred over pleurodesis. B

background.definition: A pleural effusion is an abnormal accumulation of fluid within the pleural space. A parapneumonic effusion is fluid in the pleural space secondary to pneumonia or abscess. Parapneumonic effusions can be either simple or complicated. Complicated parapneumonic effusions are defined by either the need for intervention or a positive bacterial culture. An empyema is pus within the pleural space.

list.listitem: There are an estimated 800,000 cases per year in the United States.
The prevalence in the ICU population can be as high as 62%.
A total of 20% to 57% of all patients hospitalized for community-acquired pneumonia in the United States develop parapneumonic effusion.
Overall, 74% of effusions are exudative and 26% are transudative. See below for distribution of specific causes within each of those categories:

Exudative: (1) malignancy (41%); lung, breast, ovary, stomach, lymphoma are most common; (2) tuberculosis (28%); (3) pneumonia (bacterial or viral—17%); (4) medications (amiodarone, nitrofurantoin, phenytoin, methotrexate, cyclophosphamide, penicillamine); (5) rheumatoid arthritis/autoimmune disorders; and (6) postmyocardial infarction.

Transudative: (1) congestive heart failure (72%); (2) cirrhosis (11%); (3) nephrotic syndrome (10%); (4) hypoalbuminemia (7%); and (5) other (pulmonary embolism, superior vena cava obstruction, Meigs syndrome, constrictive pericarditis, hypothyroidism).
Exudative pleural effusions develop as the result of increased pleural membrane permeability to proteins.

Transudative pleural effusions develop as the result of an imbalance of hydrostatic forces across the pleural membrane. These forces include oncotic pressure, hydrostatic pressure, and/or intrapleural pressure.
Symptoms of a pleural effusion include cough, pleuritic chest pain, and dyspnea. C

Unless heart failure is the known etiology, perform imaging guided thoracentesis for all patients with pleural fluid accumulation greater than 1 cm on lateral decubitus films. Patients with unilateral effusion should have CT to evaluate for malignancy.C

Ultrasound is superior to chest radiography for detecting fluid within the pleural space and for guiding thoracentesis. It may be useful in differentiating malignant from benign effusion, and for guiding thoracentesis. C

An effusion is exudative by Light's criteria if: (1) the ratio of protein in the pleural fluid to serum protein is greater than 0.5; (2) the ratio of the level of lactated dehydrogenase (LDH) in the pleural fluid to serum LDH is greater than 0.6; or (3) the absolute level of LDH in the pleural fluid is greater than two thirds of the upper limit of local laboratory normal value. C
Pleural cholesterol >55 mg/dl, pleural LDL >200 U/L, and pleural to serum cholesterol ratio >0.3 are all highly predictive of exudative effusion. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Exposure history, hemoptysis, positive tuberculin skin test, fevers, night sweats
Stigmata of SLE (arthritis, rash, renal disease, serositis)
Lower extremity swelling, rales, jugular venous distension, orthopnea, dyspnea on exertion
Lower extremity swelling, history of immobilization
Pericardial rub, history of streptococcal infection, renal disease, liver disease

list.listitem: Dullness to percussion and asymmetric chest expansion are the most useful physical findings in the diagnosis of pleural effusion.
The likelihood of a pleural effusion being either transudative or exudative can often be determined by history and physical examination. C
Dyspnea, cough, and pleuritic chest pain are the most common symptoms associated with pleural effusion.

Asymmetric chest expansion, reduced vocal fremitus, reduced vocal resonance, and decreased or absent breath sounds best rule in pleural effusion when present. Absence of reduced vocal fremitus or resonance and no dullness to percussion rule it out.
In patients with malignant pleural effusion, increasing levels of breathlessness are associated with worse survival.
Rarely, endometriosis can cause mostly right sided hemorrhagic pleural effusion.

The diagnosis of a pleural effusion is confirmed by chest radiography or ultrasoound. A posterioranterior chest film can detect fluid accumulation of 200 cc; a lateral decubitus film can detect accumulations as small as 50 cc.
Ultrasound is more sensitive than plain films for the detection of small pleural effusions. A study in sickle cell patients found that it compared well with CT.

British Thoracic Society guidelines (2024) recommend that all patients with unilateral effusion have CT to evaluate for malignancy. Ultrasound is a less accurate alternative in resource poor settings. It correctly diagnosed malignancy in 26/33 patients (sensitivity 73%, specificity 100%) and benign disease in 19/19. Pleural thickening >1 cm, pleural nodularity and diaphragmatic thickening >7 mm were highly suggestive of malignant disease.
Patients with unilateral effusion should have image guided thoracentesis to obtain fluid for analysis (25-50 ml).
Point of care ultrasound is endorsed by 2021 American College of Physicians guidelines for the evaluation of the patient with acute dyspnea.

Unless heart failure is the obvious source of the pleural effusion, perform image guided thoracentesis to determine the cause of the effusion for all patients with greater than 1 cm of pleural fluid layering on lateral decubitus films.
Medical thoracoscopy may be useful in detecting pleural metastases and determining the origin of exudative pleural effusions.

BTS guidelines (2024) recommend that pleural fluid analysis should include the following parameters: cell count, adenosine deaminase (to rule out tuberculosis), cytology (examination for malignant cells), protein, cholesterol, amylase, pH, gram stain, cell counts, and culture. BTS guidelines recommend IFN-gamma to test for tuberculosis in high prevalence populations, and pleural fluid ADA to rule it out in low prevalence settings. Obtain pleural fluid ANA if lupus is suspected. Serum protein and LDH should also be obtained (see ).
Tumor necrosis factor-alpha assay of pleural fluid is an accurate test for tuberculous pleurisy (sensitivity 85%, specificity 80%, AUROCC 0.89).

A systematic review of 44 studies with 4974 patients concluded that pleural fluid interferon-gamma was the most accurate test for diagnosis of tubercular pleural effusion (91% sensitive, 96% specific, LR+ 23, LR- 0.09).

Light's original criteria for identifying pleural fluid as exudative were presence of at least one of the following: (1) pleural fluid-to-serum protein ratio of >0.5, (2) pleural fluid-to-serum LDH ratio of >0.6, or (3) pleural fluid LDH concentration >two-thirds the upper limit of normal for LDH.

Other indicators of exudate include elevated pleural fluid cholesterol and elevated pleural fluid protein. A systematic review identified elevated pleural cholesterol level >55 mg/dl (LR+ 7.1-250, LR− 0.07-0.16), elevated pleural LDL >200 U/L (LR+ 18, LR− 0.32) and a pleural to serum cholesterol ratio >0.3 (LR+ 14, LR− 0.08) as the best predictors of exudative pleural effusion.

Exudates typically have protein >3 g/dL, a transudate have protein <3 g/dL. The combination of either pleural fluid LDH and pleural fluid cholesterol OR pleural fluid protein, pleural fluid cholesterol and pleural fluid LDH correlate well with Light's criteria and obviates the need to draw serum.

In a study of 289 patients with pleural effusion, a ratio of LDH to adenoine deaminase greater than 15.5 and a carcinoembryonic antigen level <5 ng/ml suggested parapneumonic effusion or empyema rather than transudative effusion due to heart or renal failure, tubercular effusion, or malignant effusion.
In one small study, the addition of hydrogen peroxide produced profuse bubbles in exudative pleural fluid and no bubbles in transudates, unless blood was present.

Among patients with pleural effusion, cytology and pleural biopsy are the most accurate tests. Elevated tumor necrosis factor and an elevated pleural to serum ratio of tumor necrosis factor also predict malignancy. CEA, CA-125, CA 15-3, and CYFRA 21-1 are highly specific for malignancy but not sensitive.
Patients with persistent effusion and no diagnosis may require bronchoscopy or pleural biopsy.

A systematic review of 7 studies with approximately 2000 patients found that a ratio of serum LDH to pleural adenosine deaminase greater than approximately 10 was 96% sensitive and 88% specific for the diagnosis of malignant pleural effusion (studies in the meta-analysis used a range of cutoffs from 5 to 20). Positive and negative likelihood ratios were 8 and 0.05 respectively.
Tumor markers such as CA 15-3, CA 125 and CA 19-9 are specific but lack sensitivity for distinguishing malignant from benign effusion.
Soluble mesothelin-related peptide (SMRP) was accurate for diagnosis of pleural effusion caused by malignant mesthelioma (LR+ 7.8, LR- 0.35) in a systematic review of 13 studies with 3359 patients.
Elevated serum c-reactive protein was associated with poor survival in patients with malignant pleural effusion.
See for a suggested approach to diagnosis.
Rapid drainage of complicated parapneumonic effusions prevents undue morbidity and mortality. C
Bilateral pleural effusions with clear clinical clues to a transudative process (eg, heart failure) need not usually be tapped. C
Admit the patient if the underlying cause of an exudative pleural effusion is not clear. Always consider malignancy, tuberculosis and pulmonary embolism. C
For malignant pleural effusion, in patients with expandable lungs either USN guided large volume thoracentesis using an indwelling cathter or talc pleurodesis are options.B
If malignant pleural effusion that is non-expandable, indwelling catheter as well as pleural aspiration, talc slurry or talc poudrage pleurodesis, or decortication surgery are options.B

Any pleural effusion (either transudative or exudative) that causes respiratory compromise should be drained by needle thoracentesis or, if necessary, by chest tube. Because of high rates of morbidity (and mortality), large pleural effusions should be drained without delay.

A clinical trial compared NSAIDs versus opiates for pain, and found similar results although a greater need for rescue medications. Smaller (12F) chest tubes were less painful than 24F tubes, but also less effective and had more complications.
Bilateral pleural effusions with clear clinical clues to a transudative process (eg, heart failure) need not be tapped.
The placement of 2 chest tubes by video-assisted thoracic surgery and general anesthesia may afford superior debridement and drainage of large and established empyemas.
There is insufficient evidence to recommend routine fibrinolysis either alone or in combination with chest tube drainage for patients with complicated parapneumonic effusions or empyema.

A systematic review of nontraumatic, noninfectious, transudative pleural effusions in mechanically ventilated critically ill adult patients identified 28 studies of mostly low quality. The authors concluded that drainage of pleural effusions in mechanically ventilated adult patients increased oxygenation and this outweighed the risk of complications such as pneumothorax. The greatest benefit was seen in patients with a PaO2:FiO2 ratio of less than 200 and a pleural effusion estimated volume of greater than 500 mL. There was not enough data to make a recommendation on the use of catheter versus needle thoracentesis for pleural fluid drainage.

An ATS guideline (2018) recommends treating symptomatic patients with malignant pleural effusion and potentially expandable lungs with ultrasound guided large volume thoracentesis using an indwelling pleural catheter or chemical pleurodesis In observational studies this technique was associated with a lower rate of pneumothorax (4% vs 9%). In patients with nonexpandable lungs, the guideline recommends indwelling pleural catheters over pleurodesis. For patients with catheter-related infection, removal of the catheter is recommended if the infection persists. If pleurodesis is chosen, talc is recommended for malignant pleural effusions.

British Thoracic Society guidelines (2024) recommend talc pleurodesis or another method of pleurodesis over multiple aspirations. For patients with expandable malignant effusion an indwelling pleural catheter or talc pleurodesis is recommended.

British Thoracic Society guidelines (2024) recommend that for a malignant pleural effusion that is non-expandable, indwelling pleural catheter should be considered as well as pleural aspiration, talc slurry or talc poudrage pleurodesis, or decortication surgery are options. Pleural aspiration may be desirable before indwelling pleural catheter to assess symptomatic responses.

An RCT randomized 149 patients with malignant pleural effusion to daily versus every other day drainage found a greater likelihood of complete or partial response (autopleurodesis) in the group with daily drainage (47% vs 24%, p = 0.003, NNT = 4). The median time to autopleurodesis was also significantly shorter (54 vs 90 days).

A randomized trial in 154 outpatients with malignant pleural effusion inserted an indwelling catheter for regular outpatient drainage. If there was no evidence of lung entrapment at 10 days, they were randomized to talc slurry or placebo. After 35 days, successful pleurodesis was more likely in the talc group (43% vs 23%, p = 0.008, NNT = 5).

An RCT in the UK randomized 330 adults with malignant pleural effusion to either (1) local anesthetic thoracoscopy and talc poudrage or (2) talc slurry via a chest tube. At 3 months, dthere were no ifferences between groups in any outcomes including pleurodesis failure, mortality, complications, or length of stay. Thoracoscopy based therapy was unlikely to be cost-effective based on their analysis.

A RCT compared chest tube insertion with talc pleurodesis against indwelling pleural catheters (IPC) among 106 patients with a malignant pleural effusion. It demonstrated that IPC was associated with fewer hospital days (−3.5 days) and fewer follow up procedures (6% vs 20%) but higher rate of pleural based infection (9.6% vs 1.9%). There were no between group differences in quality of life scores or dyspnea scores.

The Chinese herbal medicine elemene is widely used in China. A systematic review of 46 small clinical trials with a total of 2992 patients reported that its use was associated with a greater likelihood of complete resolution of the effusion (RR 1.37, 95% CI 1.23-1.52). However, all of the trials were unblinded with unconcealed allocation to groups, and not all were randomized.

Treat pleural effusions by correcting underlying cause. For transudative pleural effusions, in particular, control of the underlying disease process (heart failure, cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome), facilitates resolution of the pleural effusion.
In a RCT of 360 patients undergoing cardiac surgery, colchicine therapy given for one month post-operatively, significantly reduced the incidence of post-operative pleural effusions (12.2% vs 25.6%).

Combined therapy with both intrapleural DNase and tissue plasminogen activator (t-PA) in patients with a pleural infection is designed to improve pleural fluid drainage. It was associated with a lower frequency of surgical referral and a reduction in length of hospital stay compared to placebo or either agent alone.
Admit the patient if the underlying cause of an exudative pleural effusion is not clear. Always consider tuberculosis and pulmonary embolism.
Admit—and refer appropriately—those patients for whom drainage, pleurodesis, thoracoscopy, or surgery is indicated.
Surgical consultation is indicated in patients with parapneumonic effusions, if conservative therapy has not resulted in clinical or radiographic improvement within 3 days.
Acute lung injury can occur after talc pleurodesis. Consider avoiding talc pleurodesis on patients who have recently had chemotherapy or who are using supplemental oxygen.
Chest pain is commonly associated with pleurodesis and can be treated with systemic analgesics or intrapleural lidocaine.
Malignant pleural effusions are associated with shortened survival in cancer patients. B
Even with surgical drainage, mortality rates of empyema approach 20%. B

Patients who have pneumonia with an associated parapneumonic effusion have elevated mortality compared with patients who have pneumonia without effusion (relative risk = 6.5, if bilateral; 3.7, if unilateral). B

In a Spanish study, use of a rapid immunochromatographic test for the detection of pneumococcal antigen in pleural fluid of children had a relatively high sensitivity and specificity (88% and 71%, respectively) with a positive predictive value of 96%.

cell.label: Pleural effusion without heart failure as clear cause. Perform thoracentesis and analyze for LDH, protein, and cholesterol. Draw serum LDH, protein, cholesterol. Empyema, chylothorax, or hemothorax?
Pleural:serum protein >0.5 OR pleural:serum LDH >0.6 OR pleural LDH >2/3 ULN of serum LDH OR pleural cholesterol >80 mg/dL or pleural protein >4.0 mg/dL?
Transudate. Consider heart failure, nephrosis, cirrhosis.
Exudate. Obtain pleural fluid glucose, ADA, cell counts, amylase, cytology, pH, and culture.
Consider bronchoscopy or pleural biopsy if not improving.
Malignancy (cytology), infection (culture), or pancreatic pleural effusion or esophageal rupture (amylase).
Not exudate or transudate. Order additional studies for underlying cause (infection, malignancy).
